stories.title: Nepal floods: What foreign travellers need to know
stories.summary: European governments have issued safety guidance and emergency contacts for travellers as flooding and landslides disrupt transport across parts of Nepal. Hundreds of foreign tourists are reported missing after devastating flooding in Nepal struck an area popular with international travellers. The Nepal Tourism Board said on Thursday that 590 tourists were out of contact, including 476 foreign nationals and 114 Nepalis, according to figures reported by the Kathmandu Post. They include visitors from the United States, Australia, the UK, Germany and the numbers are rising. The disaster has particularly affected Rasuwa and neighbouring Nuwakot, north of Kathmandu and close to Nepal's border with Tibet. The country is home to eight of the world's 10 highest mountains, including Mount Everest, and official figures show 1.16 million international tourists visited Nepal in 2025, including more than 165,000 who went trekking. What should travellers in Nepal do? European governments and other foreign embassies are advising travellers to follow instructions from Nepalese authorities and closely monitor local conditions. The embassies of Finland, France and the UK, together with Australia, Norway and Switzerland and the EU Delegation in Nepal, issued a joint statement urging people in affected areas to "follow the guidance of local authorities and official safety advisories as the situation continues to evolve". France warns that due to flooding and landslides telephone networks and internet connections can be cut for several days. Travellers are advised to check with local authorities before making journeys and to follow their instructions. The Netherlands advises people caught in flooding to move to higher ground, avoid bridges and not attempt to walk or swim through floodwater.

stories.title: Japan to probe popular animal cafes amid hygiene, welfare concerns
stories.summary: Japan plans to look into popular animal cafes, where visitors can interact with anything from cats to capybaras, following concerns about hygiene and the creatures’ welfare, authorities said on Thursday. Japan has hundreds of the cafes where campaigners say animals are sometimes kept in cramped spaces, and that their popularity encourages the capture and illegal trade of rare wildlife.
